TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
TUESDAY, 12 MAY 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEDT)
DAY 7
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC, COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC WITH ZELIE HEGER SC AND
TAMARA PHILLIPS, COUNSEL ASSISTING

<THE HEARING RESUMED AT 10.00 AM
MS HEGER SC: Commissioner, the first witness I intended to call this morning is
Emeritus Professor Andrew Markus.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, perhaps before that, I think we have Ms Dwyer here.
MS DWYER SC: May it please the Commission, with the Commission's leave
I appear on behalf of the Jewish Council of Australia. I appear with my learned
friend Ms Fain-Vallantin and behind me Mr Hartley and we have the Executive
Director of the Jewish Council of Australia present.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, very well, I confirm the grant of limited leave that I
announced at the commencement of this hearing block, Ms Dwyer. I might just take
you - do you have the application before you so I can just indicate the extent of the
grant.
MS DWYER SC: Yes, your Honour.
COMMISSIONER: If I go to paragraph 12, and subparagraphs (1), (2), (3), (4), (5),
(6) are the subject of the grant. To the extent that Professor Markus is able to
comment on (7), that is the subject of the grant.
MS HEGER SC: I just wish to confirm we are both looking at the same document.
The application by the Jewish Council of Australia, paragraph 11 -
COMMISSIONER: I am sorry.
MS HEGER SC: - that sets out the topics on which they seek leave to examine
Professor Markus.
COMMISSIONER: My apologies, Ms Heger and Ms Dwyer. How confusing that
must have been. A loose document in the front of my folder was a reference to
a different document. My apologies indeed to you and to counsel for the Executive
Council of Australian Jewry, Ms Hillman. We will start again, Ms Dwyer, and let's
hope we get it right this time.
The grant - I'm referring now to paragraph 11, subparagraphs (1), (2), (3), (4) are the
subject of the grant. Professor Markus' expertise is in the conduct of surveys of this
kind. Professor Markus' view on the importance of free speech do not seem to me to
fall within the area of his expertise. To the extent you are testing the subscale of
anti-Zionism, Ms Dwyer, that is within the grant but any broader discussion of the
right to free expression of political views or the like seems to me to fall outside the
grant.
And, in a sense, that same caution applies to subparagraph (6). Subparagraph (7)
seems to me plainly outside the grant. To the extent it is within his expertise,

subparagraph (9) is in. I note the suggestion that you might cross-examine on the
documents identified in paragraph 17.
MS DWYER SC: We are no longer going to do that, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: That's not pressed? Fine.
MS DWYER SC: If I can give you some comfort, I've discussed this with Counsel
Assisting this morning, and we take it as uncontroversial that people are entitled to
express political views without being labelled antisemitic, and we focus very much
on the surveys.
COMMISSIONER: Very well. Now, the second matter, Ms Dwyer, before I go to
Ms Hillman, is I am aware that the council would like to cross-examine Dr Oboler,
who I am expecting we will hear from a little later in the morning, and I understand
that in terms of the late service of the document, that's just not practical and I accept
that. I trust Dr Oboler will be forgiving when I say that the intention is that he return
in a later segment to give some further evidence, a segment that will be devoted to
the question of the online environment, and on that occasion, Ms Dwyer, you may
expect that you will have leave to cross-examine on Dr Oboler's evidence respecting
prevalence in the surveys for which he is responsible.
MS DWYER SC: We are very grateful for that, thank you, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you, Ms Dwyer. Ms Hillman, needless to say, the
Executive Council has leave to examine Professor Markus on all the areas that are
the subject of the grant of leave to the Jewish Council and, indeed, Ms Hillman if
there are further areas, I will hear you on that.
MS HILLMAN: Thank you, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: It might be Mr Zwier wants to have a word with you.
MS HILLMAN: Mr Zwier reminds me, Commissioner, I expect that the leave is
behalf of all of the clients, not only the ECAJ.
COMMISSIONER: I'm sorry, I didn't quite catch that.
MS HILLMAN: The leave grant is for all of the clients represented by Arnold
Bloch Leibler, not just the ECAJ, I take it, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you, Mr Zwier. It is.
MS HILLMAN: Thank you, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, very well. Yes, Ms Heger.

MS HEGER SC: Commissioner, I now call Emeritus Andrew Markus.
<ANDREW MARKUS, SWORN
COMMISSIONER: Thank you, Professor, do take a seat.
MS HEGER SC: Professor Markus could you please state your name for the record.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Andrew Markus.
MS HEGER SC: And you have prepared an expert report for the purposes of the
Commission dated 6 May 2026; correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That's correct.
MS HEGER SC: Do you have a copy of that report there in front of you?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: I do.
MS HEGER SC: I understand there is a correction you would like to make to
paragraph 68 of the report; is that right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That is correct.
MS HEGER SC: What is that correction?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: At the bottom of 68 where it says, "don't know",
"don't know" was not an option, so it has to be crossed out.
MS HEGER SC: So we strike out the words, "and don't know". With that correction
made, is the report otherwise still true and correct to the best of your knowledge?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: I think there's table 8.3.
MS HEGER SC: Table 8.3?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: I think "don't know" and "prefer not to say" are in
the wrong way around.
MS HEGER SC: So that's on page 21 and we should reverse the order?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: So are we reversing the rows in their entirety or just the words
"don't know" and "prefer not to say"? As in should the numbers stay where they are,
and we're just switching the name?

PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: No, the numbers - so 11, 2, 35 is "don't know".
MS HEGER SC: I understand.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: And 0, 4, 1 is "prefer not to say".
MS HEGER SC: I understand. With those corrections made, is the report otherwise
true and correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: I tender that report, which is STAT.8999.0055.0012.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. The report will be Exhibit 1-112.
<EXHIBIT 1-112 EXPERT REPORT OF EMERITUS PROFESSOR
MARKUS DATED 06/05/2026
MS HEGER SC: And there's an annexure, STAT.8999.0057.0019. I tender that.
COMMISSIONER: Exhibit 1-113.
<EXHIBIT 1-113 ANNEXURE 1 TO EXPERT REPORT OF EMERITUS
PROFESSOR MARKUS
MS HEGER SC: The next annexure is STAT.8999.0057.0020. I tender that.
COMMISSIONER: That will be Exhibit 1-114.
<EXHIBIT-114 ANNEXURE 2 TO EXPERT REPORT OF EMERITUS
PROFESSOR MARKUS
MS HEGER SC: And the final annexure STAT.8999.0057.0021, I tender that.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Exhibit 1-115.
<EXHIBIT 1-115 ANNEXURE 3 TO EXPERT REPORT OF EMERITUS
PROFESSOR MARKUS
MS HEGER SC: Professor, you are an Emeritus Professor of Jewish Civilisation at
Monash University; correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And you are also a Fellow of the Academy of Social Sciences of
Australia; correct?

PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And you have experience in large-scale public opinion and social
survey research; is that right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes, that's correct.
MS HEGER SC: You have previously conducted the Scanlon Foundation Mapping
Social Cohesion series between 2009 and 2021; correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Starting in 2007.
MS HEGER SC: From 2007 to 2021; is that right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: But others took over that survey from 2022 onwards.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes, I am still involved. There's a sort of advisory
group and I'm still involved in the advisory group.
MS HEGER SC: All right. But no longer an author of the report.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: No longer.
MS HEGER SC: You have also previously led two national surveys of attitudes
within the Jewish community; the first known as Gen08, and that was in 2007 to
2008; correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: And the second was known as Gen17 conducted in 2017?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: And you've also conducted surveys of Australian attitudes towards
the Jewish community; correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That is correct.
MS HEGER SC: The first being Crossroads21.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And, of course, last year Crossroads25.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.

MS HEGER SC: In your report, you commence by referring to the Scanlon
Foundation surveys from about paragraph 28 and you note that that survey tracked
attitudes to Jewish Australians as well as other faith groups, including Buddhists,
Christians, Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes, that is correct.
MS HEGER SC: You note that in that survey a question was asked:
"Is your personal attitude positive, negative or neutral towards..."
the relevant faith group. Correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That is correct.
MS HEGER SC: And you note several findings from that survey. The first being
that a relatively small proportion of respondents, that is 15 per cent in 2025,
indicated they are negative towards people of Jewish faith. Correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That is correct.
MS HEGER SC: And you - the second point you make is that that was marginally
lower than the proportion indicating a negative attitude towards other faith groups,
with the exception of Hindus which had 14 per cent; correct? And Buddhists at four
per cent. Is that right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes, and one group was higher.
MS HEGER SC: That being the Muslim group, which was at 35 per cent; correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And the third point you note is that the proportion of respondents
to this question expressing a negative attitude towards people of Jewish faith
increased since 2023 from nine per cent to 15 per cent; correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes. I think that's a very important context because
if you just have that finding on its own, you would have a different understanding
than if you understood that there was a general movement for most faith groups.
MS HEGER SC: So that movement was reflected across other faith groups as well?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes and that shows that if you only have something
in isolation, you may misinterpret what is happening.

MS HEGER SC: The fourth point you note as far as that Scanlon Foundation survey
is concerned is that an examination of the full response range shows a higher
proportion of "neutral" and a small proportion of "don't know" responses in relation
to attitudes towards people of the Jewish faith. Do you consider those non-committal
responses significant?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: I think the data is uneven because there is a table,
table 1, which shows that there is some variation for faith groups from 44 per cent to
59 per cent and possibly not a simple and clear explanation of that. I think the main
point there is to understand that the way that - if when people are asked about faith
groups, a lot of people will say, "Well, I don't have a view on that. I'm neutral." The
old Australians say, you know, "That's not my business."
MS HEGER SC: Now, you yourself did not conduct that particular survey. That
was the one from 2025; correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes, that is correct.
MS HEGER SC: But you considered it relevant as providing context for explaining
the Crossroads25 findings; is that right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes. You see, these surveys are the best, almost, that
are conducted in Australia. There are some government surveys that have very large
samples like 30,000 but there's very few of them. And in the private sector there's
very few surveys using a probability sample with such a large respondents, it's
8000-plus in 2025. So I think that's particularly interesting because it is as good an
indication as we can have of attitudes to Jewish Australians, albeit that it is in the
context of faith groups.
MS HEGER SC: And we will come to the findings from the Crossroads25 survey in
a moment but do you consider what emerges from that scan done foundation survey
is consistent with the results of the Crossroads25 survey?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: I believe it is consistent and, you know, you're
getting a lot of indications of negativity in the 15 to 20 per cent range with a lot of
these questions. So in many of the Scanlon, many of the Crossroads25 questions,
there are 12 items, and 11 of those items would be within that range, or lower. So
I do think that that is an important cross-validation, particularly in the context that
there are some other surveys discussed in this report, which would indicate a high
level of negativity. So that, I think, is why it's an important benchmark.
MS HEGER SC: I understand. As I say, we will come to the particular results of
Crossroads25 in a moment. But just to understand the purpose of that survey and the
methodology you adopted, this was a survey you conducted between 5 and 25
August in the last year; is that right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Correct, yes.

MS HEGER SC: You say it was commissioned by the Jewish Independent?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: Did they have any control over the design and conduct of the
survey?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Not at all. It was total independence on my part. It's
the third survey I've done, I think, for them and I have total freedom of how to design
that.
MS HEGER SC: And you describe the Crossroads25 survey as an attitudinal
survey. Does that simply mean it's a survey that seeks to ascertain attitudes and, in
this case, attitudes towards the Jewish community?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That is correct, yes.
MS HEGER SC: And you express your aim in this report of that Crossroads25
survey as being to understand whether increased antisemitic incidents reflected
a shift in public opinion towards Jewish Australians. Is that the aim?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That is correct.
MS HEGER SC: Could you just describe for us why attitudinal surveys are useful
and also what their limitations might be compared to other forms of research?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: It's a big question. I think they are useful because
when you have people talking about, say, lived experience, which is of course
fundamental importance to listen to people, but they would not necessarily have an
overview. They might. They might say: Look I go to university every day and this is
what I see every day. That's a reflection on the broader environment, yes.
But often they're very personal, and so - not to say one approach is any better than
the other but they are complementary. And here they are complementary because
they give you an understanding of the lie of the land, and this is essentially what this
survey is about. And what the Commission may or may not find useful is having that
perspective of roughly what is the distribution of attitudes.
MS HEGER SC: And the limitations of a survey like this, I take it one limitation
you have identified is that they don't tell you everything about the experience of
antisemitism.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes. Like, surveys are very difficult to interpret.
They may be easy to interpret in terms of significance. Significance in looking at
surveys would be, has this variation happening by chance or is there some significant
element in that, and you determine the significance in terms of the sample size and

the subsample that you're looking at and so on, and is this different from that. Like, is
attitudes to Christians different to attitudes to Jews at a significant level or not. Yep.
But the big problem with surveys is they are so dependent on the exact wording of
the questions. So you get quite a whole range, if you are exploring one issue, from
the wording of the question. So I'm never hung up on the wording of a particular
question. What I'm looking for is the pattern, and the importance of trying to discern
the sort of patterns. So in this discussion, there's quite considerable discussions of
patterns, and we can look at that if you think appropriate later on. But that's the
challenge of surveying.
The order of questions can make a big difference. If you have a particular question
early in the survey, that may influence how people answer later in the survey and so
on. So in this report, there are a number of examples of the problems that you can
have in surveying which I won't traverse until there's something of particular
significance here. But I would just emphasise that what I am looking for in a survey
is not the answer to a particular question, but it is the pattern of response, the
probabilities. Does this go with that? Those sort of issues.
What I like to say with surveying is that if what you are getting is noise, meaning
when you disaggregate the findings, for example, by age group, and it is all over the
place. You know, there's no clear pattern. I think there is patterns in societies. There's
patterns in populations and surveys help you understand that pattern. And when the
survey is not working well - not always but generally it may well be that there's
something wrong here, something has happened.
For example, if I may just go on very briefly. I have had the experience of doing
probability-based surveys and non-probability based surveys, and I've had the
experience of being able to compare the two. And it really highlights the challenge of
non-probability surveying because you may not have a good sample.
MS HEGER SC: I understand. Can I ask you about the design of the survey
instrument. You personally designed it; is that right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: No, I did not.
MS HEGER SC: All right.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: It depends on what we're talking about. If we're
talking about the generalised antisemitism scale, I did not design that.
MS HEGER SC: No, I'm not talking about the scale. I'm talking about the series of
questions that were put in the survey.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: (Indistinct) survey - sorry?
MS HEGER SC: You designed the content and form of the questions.

PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That is correct.
MS HEGER SC: Drawing upon the antisemitism subscale.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That is correct.
MS HEGER SC: Which was developed by others, the antisemitism scale.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes, it was developed by others.
MS HEGER SC: And could you just describe for us what that generalised
antisemitism scale is?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yep. So that was developed by British academics
and they are academics who work in this field. They are much more in the
quantitative side of this discipline. Whereas I'm much more on the humanist side,
like, my training is as a historian. I'm not a statistician. I work with statisticians but
I'm not a statistician. And I think I bring some value to the survey in that regard
because I'm looking for meaning in fundamental things rather than in the statistical
sense.
Now, just so that people understand how surveys - quality surveys are constructed
and we're talking about this scale. It's a very lengthy process. It could take six
months or more. Like, in the Social Research Centre we were involved in
redesigning our Index of Social Cohesion and we probably spent at least six months
on that and what you would do is you would look at a number of questions that are
being used in this field. It might be 50 questions. And you would refine those
questions by a process known as factor analysis, and other processes as well.
MS HEGER SC: You are now talking about the development of the antisemitism
scale as opposed to this particular survey?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: I understand.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes. So just very briefly so it would be the statistics
that would tell you that these questions go together. That question doesn't go
together. So there might be a question which is an outlier and it doesn't actually
correlate with the other questions. That would be a basis for excluding that. And
I won't go into the statistics but there are obviously other ways - many other ways of
testing the validity of a scale.
MS HEGER SC: All right. There are two aspects to that antisemitism scale. One is
called the Judeophobic antisemitism subscale, and as you describe at paragraph 39,
that's intended to capture what you call the old antisemitism. That is, it measures

endorsement of traditional or classic prejudicial attitudes towards Jews as a group. Is
that right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That's right.
MS HEGER SC: And it also comprises what's termed the anti-Zionist antisemitism
subscale which you describe as the new antisemitism, which seeks to measure
endorsement of antisemitic attitudes directed at Israel and its supporters. Is that
right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That is correct.
MS HEGER SC: Can I then ask you about the questions that were actually included
in the survey that you designed, and they appear at annexure 2 to your report from
page 34.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: Am I right in thinking that question 2, which lists a series of
statements 1 to 10, those are drawn from the Judeophobic subscale?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Not exactly because there's 10 questions there and
six questions are in the actual scale. These other questions were derived largely from
a Canadian survey conducted by Professor Robert Brim of the University of Toronto
and he used 10 questions. And we tried to add some other questions to see if that
would improve the scale. And we've just been recently doing some work - not me,
but a statistician colleague - and it didn't really - these additional questions did not
improve the validity of the scale in the statistical sense. So that the report that
I prepared uses the six questions that are in the subscale developed by the British
academics.
MS HEGER SC: If we want to understand the six questions are, those are set out in
table 2 of your report; is that right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: So that table lists the six questions from the Judeophobic subscale;
correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: I'm just trying to find it.
MS HEGER SC: It's around about page 14.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes, table 2. Yes, that is correct.
MS HEGER SC: I understand. And then question 4 in the survey instrument, which
appears on page 35, that is again partly drawing from the anti-Zionist subscale?

PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: It has the six items -
MS HEGER SC: Yes.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: - in the subscale plus the additional ones based on
the Canadian research.
MS HEGER SC: And so if we want to understand what were the questions from the
anti-Zionist subscale, that's represented in table 3.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: On page 15 of your report; is that right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: And so did you find that the additional questions you included in
the survey instrument were not valid in the same way you reached that conclusion for
the additional questions for the first set of questions?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: They were to some extent but I did not think that
they were necessary of this report. So I used a couple of those questions. For
example, one of the questions was "...Israel is apartheid state".
MS HEGER SC: That's a question that you added that wasn't from the
anti-Zionist subscale?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: So why did you add that question?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Just to test what impact that might have, what sort of
response we would get, and what we found was with a very abstract question like
that, the proportion of people saying "don't know", or that category of response, went
up - I think 60 per cent or so just from memory but it's in here, with regard to that
question. You can find it exactly - yes, this is table 4, page 17, "...Israel is an
apartheid state", 62 per cent of people did not give a substantive response to that
question.
So, to me, what that says is that regard to the general population, there's one group of
people who are not interested; it's not their business. And there's another group who
don't know. You know, in a way, there's so much richness in this survey that I've got
written here 30 pages. We could easily write 130 pages on this. Because, for
example, there are differences between men and women and how men and women
answer a question about knowledge. But I thought for the purposes of this report
which is to give the broad lie of the land, it was not necessary to go into that detail.

MS HEGER SC: All right. So, if we then focus on the questions from the
anti-Zionist subscale set out at table 3 at page 15 of your report, can I just seek to
understand the purpose behind some of these questions. So the first question that's
listed there:
"I am comfortable spending time with people who openly support Israel."
People had the option of disagreeing, strongly agreeing, agreeing or strongly
agreeing or offering some more non-committal answers; is that right?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes, that's right.
MS HEGER SC: And so by including that question, say someone disagrees or
strongly disagrees with that statement, in other words they are saying they're not
comfortable spending time with people who openly support Israel, are you
suggesting the person who answers that in that way is necessarily antisemitic?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Not at all, no.
MS HEGER SC: So what is the purpose of including that question then?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Well, you see, that mirrors the question in the
Judeophobic scale:
"I am just as open to having Jewish friends..."
That is still on page 15. So that mirrors that. But at the end of the day, I just really
make two points. I think it's a mistake to fixate on one question because what we're
looking at is the pattern of response. Because there may be the way that people
interpret that question. The larger the sample and the more robust the scale, the more
chance you've got of getting something meaningful.
And so what I would say that is meaningful there is that it was three per cent in
general terms. It's gone up to 16 per cent. So that might indicate like a 13 per cent
increase when we ask them that in the context of Israel. And it just points us in the
direction, without being able to clearly establish the meaning at this stage, of the
impact of those questions to do with Israel as opposed to questions in general terms.
MS HEGER SC: So you're more interested in how people's responses to these
questions change over time and also how their responses to one question might line
up with a response to another question, for example.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes. So you can see a clear pattern of the way that
people are responding to that. So the strongest is when:
"Israel treats the Palestinians like the Nazis treated the Jews."

And you see, that's almost an outlier, isn't it, because with other questions, 20 per
cent was the highest you got. There, you've got 33 per cent. And the purpose of that
is not to close the discussion but to open the discussion. What does that mean? And it
doesn't mean if you endorse that you are antisemitic. I'm not really necessarily
interested in that. I'm interested in the pattern of response and what happens to the
pattern of response when you introduce Israel into the questions.
MS HEGER SC: All right. We will come to some more of your findings in more
detail shortly to draw that out but just for completeness, I would ask you the same
question in respect of the question you have included there:
"Israel and its supporters are a bad influence on our democracy."
If someone agrees or strongly agrees with that statement, again, you're not
suggesting that that is a necessarily antisemitic position?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Not at all. It's part of the matrix that we put together
and try and get meaning out of that. And also I would add, that's my meaning.
I always - because often when you get surveys reported, people don't give you full
frequencies. So you can see there's a lot of reports in my table and I - when we
released this, we also released the full questionnaire. Many other surveys, you get top
line findings. Here I'm presenting this data and it's for us to think about. My aim is
for the Commission to think about these issues. Is there substance, are we learning
anything from this or is this just gobbledegook?
MS HEGER SC: I take it, then, to the extent anyone agrees with negative
statements with Israel set out in this table, you're not suggesting they're necessarily
being antisemitic?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Not at all.
MS HEGER SC: I understand.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: We do know what antisemitism means and you last
week, I think, were - I wouldn't say introduced to it because it's not something new,
but you were certainly understood what antisemitism means in practice. This is not
about antisemitism, this or that. It's about the pattern and how does society work, for
example, how do young people answer those questions? How do people of
a particular political persuasion answer that question? Are there patterns or not?
MS HEGER SC: I understand. Can I ask you then about the method for conducting
the survey, again, before coming to some of the particular findings. So the survey
was conducted using the YouGov survey company; correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: That's correct.

MS HEGER SC: And they have a research panel including 71,000 individuals who
have agreed to take part in surveys; correct?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes, that's correct.
MS HEGER SC: But this particular survey, Crossroads25, was completed by 2270
respondents.
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And on your understanding, is the selection of those 2270 out of
the 71,000, that's not totally random selection, it is? Is it targeted in some way?
PROFESSOR MARKUS AO: It's targeted in the sense that the survey company

do that on an ongoing basis or whether to actually move so that they would have the
option to send their son to a different public school.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've described a different public school example, this time

MS PHILLIPS: Do you understand that this other boy was another primary school

MS GOLDMAN: That's correct. He was another 10-year-old boy in his year. This

being held at home, and then school holidays commenced. I sought to engage with
the school because the approach I take is, firstly, to ensure the school is aware of the
incident and managing it appropriately. That there are, of course, consequences and
appropriate disciplinary procedures. But also importantly using it as an opportunity
for learning. As I say, it's action learning. What better way to talk about what is

when you have got live examples that the children can relate to. But it took many
months to actually get a meeting with the school. When we finally did, we met with

schools to deal with racism.

students on an excursion to the Sydney Jewish Museum and to utilise resources that
we offered to make available that could be incorporated in education. Unfortunately,
the student returned to school at the beginning of semester 3 and the same bullying
behaviours were repeated. So after a few days, the mother pulled him out of school,
home schooled him for a semester while she then worked out another school that he

could attend. So I think this example shows that when things aren't addressed swiftly
and effectively, these problems continue to perpetuate and nothing is done to change
the conditions, whether it be naivety, ignorance or malicious intention, to actually
address the situation.
And I think the other point I would make here is whilst there are many examples like
this and they all differ in some way, shape or form, the Jewish Board of Deputies is
not resourced to be able to address this across every school in which antisemitic
incidents are occurring, and while we are to provide emotional support to the parents
and to endeavour to connect principals to education, a more systemic solution is
needed.
MS PHILLIPS: And you made the note in your statement that even where there
might be positive outcomes, they shouldn't require, for that to occur, the Jewish
Board of Deputies to have to intervene. Does that remain your view?
MS GOLDMAN: Absolutely. I think it's a failure on our society if these kinds of

identified and when an institution like the Jewish Board of Deputies is brought into
the equation. And there aren't always going to be Jewish students or Jewish teachers
present to be the marker of where antisemitism is occurring. There are many schools
that would have no Jewish students. So we need a systemic, broad solution that will
ensure schools are addressing antisemitism at the early stages and preventing it from
occurring in the future.

MS GOLDMAN: So we were contacted by a woman who had two young daughters
